name: Native American Animism
line: Relate to land, animals and weather as kin.
era: Many nations, oral traditions over thousands of years

quote.text: Mitákuye Oyás’iŋ: we are all related.

practices.name: Learn one plant or animal by name

tasks.name: Find whose land you live on
tasks.meta: Learn the nation’s name and language

tasks.name: Give something back
tasks.meta: Clean a path, plant, feed birds

rules.text: Say thank you aloud to what feeds you
Do not imitate sacred ceremonies you were not invited to
Listen before you speak, especially to elders

watch.title: Reservation Dogs
watch.creator: Series by Sterlin Harjo and Taika Waititi

listen.title: Native-led radio and podcasts
listen.creator: Start with one nation’s own station

customs.title: Offer thanks before eating
customs.creator: Name where the food came from

customs.title: Learn the land acknowledgment as a first lesson
customs.creator: Then ask what you can do

ethics.title: Reciprocity
ethics.text: Receive gifts from the land, and give something back.

ethics.title: Kinship with all beings
ethics.text: People, animals, plants and rivers are relatives, not resources.

ethics.title: Respect cultural protocols
ethics.text: Some ceremonies are not for outsiders. Learn, do not take.

philosophy.title: Place as teacher
philosophy.text: Knowledge is bound to land, season and story.

philosophy.title: Seven generations
philosophy.text: Decide with those seven generations ahead in mind (Haudenosaunee).

philosophy.title: Gratitude as a way of seeing
philosophy.text: Giving thanks changes what you notice.

journal: What did you give thanks for today, and to whom?
What did your sit spot show you today?
What took more than you gave back?
What did you learn about the place you live?
Who is an elder in your life, and what have you asked them?
Where did you treat something as a resource, not a relative?
What would seven generations from now say about today?
reflect: What changed when you named everything as kin?
Which practice changed you the most, and why?
How will you keep giving back to the place you live?

intro: There is no single Native American religion. Hundreds of nations hold distinct languages, stories and practices. Many share a view of the world as a web of relationships among people, animals, plants, waters and places.
This Onda is an invitation to listen and learn, not to imitate. Prefer Indigenous-authored sources and support nations directly.

history.what: Hundreds of nations live across the continent with distinct governance and ceremony
The Haudenosaunee Confederacy forms, by oral account, around the Great Law of Peace
The American Indian Religious Freedom Act is passed in the United States
Language and ceremony revitalization led by Native communities

concepts.text: All beings are relatives with obligations.
Taking and giving are one practice.
Law, history and teaching are carried by speakers.
Words hold local knowledge that translation loses.

facts.text: Many Indigenous languages have no word for religion as a separate part of life.
The Three Sisters, corn, beans and squash, are planted together to help each other grow.
Some ceremonies are closed. Respecting that is part of the practice.
